a106.speaker: Social media posts (unattributed)
a106.speech: Alleged on Sunday that 11 had been recaptured, contrary to the report.

a145.speaker: Aaron Motsoaledi, South African Health Minister
a145.speech: Said last month that 520 700 extra previously diagnosed people with HIV have been started on treatment since the end of February, and that in his words the department has reached “more than 50% of the target” they set out to achieve by the end of the year ; “The reason that we [were] able to reach half a million within a short space of time, was because of weekly check-in meetings with provinces, where reports that come from the ground are verified in the presence of all provincial colleagues before they are regarded as final figures for reporting.”

a145.speaker: Study from the Western Cape
a145.speech: Shows that close to half of people on medication stop at least once, and that some even pause and then restart up to three times.

a145.speaker: Kate Rees, public health specialist at the Anova Health Institute
a145.speech: “Getting that last one million or so people on treatment is not simple”; says part of the reason is that a large proportion of the group needed to close the gap are people who have been on ARVs before but have since stopped ; explains that people miss refill appointments because they can’t afford time off work or have moved province or district, and that the longer the interruption lasts the more hesitant people are to go back because they dread being treated poorly or getting “kicked to the back of the queue”, with sex workers, trans folk or men who have sex with men facing judgment ; “The health service expects people to be very rigid with their appointments, but life just is not like that.”

a145.speaker: Kate Rees, public health specialist at the Anova Health Institute
a145.speech: “There will always be people who interrupt their treatment. It’s not possible to keep everyone perfectly in the system all the time — that’s life”; says what is important is to make those pauses as short as possible by helping people get back on medication quickly and easily — without judgment.

a145.speaker: Leigh Johnson, one of the lead developers of the Thembisa model
a145.speech: Says it’s best to look at the difference in the total number of people on HIV treatment from year to year to get a sense of progress towards the UN’s second 95-95-95 target ; says current forecasts from the model are that the total number on treatment will grow by only about 160 000 this year, but that this is based on programmes running like they have up to now and, with recent upsets because of US funding cuts, it may be an unreasonable assumption.

a145.speaker: Thembisa model (data)
a145.speech: Numbers show that in 2023 roughly 793 500 people who had been on treatment before weren’t any longer, but about 728 000 who received medication were restarters; data also shows that over the years the number of people starting medication for the first time has shrunk while counts of restarters have grown.

a145.speaker: Gesine Meyer-Rath, health economist at HE2RO, University of the Witwatersrand
a145.speech: Agrees with Rees; says her group’s analyses have shown that honing in on keeping people on HIV treatment is the best way to go — especially now that funding is shrinking — and that “we can close the 1.1-million gap through improved retention alone” ; explains that to plan sensibly policymakers should know how many people are first-time starters, how many pause and restart, and how many stop and don’t come back ; “The more detail programme planners have in the data, the better. The [government’s] ‘Close the Gap’ campaign has a lot of good ideas, but having the right numbers of where the gap is that we want to close is crucial, as is keeping these numbers accurate as we progress.”

a145.speaker: Gesine Meyer-Rath, health economist at HE2RO, University of the Witwatersrand
a145.speech: “The less data we have, the more we’re flying blind, which leaves space for bickering over the data that is still there.”

a145.speaker: Bhekisisa (report)
a145.speech: Reported last month that because of the US’s aid withdrawal about 40% of South Africa’s HIV data capturers will likely have lost their jobs by September.

a303.speaker: Assa Badiallo Toure, Malian Minister of Health and Social Development
a303.speech: Recalled that the government of Mali has committed to increasing the budget allocated to covering caesarean sections, to the tune of 1,347,742,000 CFA francs, a coverage rate of 24.9%, and that from 2005 to 2023 the number of women delivered by caesarean section rose from 4,300 to 40,527; welcoming the cooperation shown by the donation, she expressed her satisfaction at the prospects of extending obstetric interventions to about 2,000 women of childbearing age in the short term and to 12,125 patients in the subsequent stages of the programme.

a303.speaker: Mohamed Lemine Mohamed Beiba, UNFPA Representative in Mali
a303.speech: Said this event marks the first stage of a gradual process of handing over kits making it possible to carry out around 2,000 caesarean sections in optimal health-safety conditions, and that in the coming months a second phase will complete the need in order to reach a total of 12,125 caesarean sections, about 30% of total annual needs.

a303.speaker: Rachna Korhonen, United States Ambassador to Mali
a303.speech: Said this support in kits is certainly an important step but does not cover Mali's needs; announced that reflections are under way to respond further to needs, notably in blood transfusion kits, for the next two years.

a315.speaker: Rogério Zandamela, Governor of the Bank of Mozambique
a315.speech: Regretted the decision by Standard & Poor's to lower the rating of domestic public debt issues to selective default, admitting it had an impact on access to credit: “It means that we are left with an almost speculative debt instrument. If it's speculative, few investors will want to hold that bond, that instrument, in their portfolio.” ; “It undermines investor confidence. This has implications for access to external credit for families, companies and the state” ; said measures are needed to “within a reasonable time period” be able to “raise the rating” again, and emphasised the possibility that some investors may want to “get rid” of the Mozambican debt securities they hold.

a315.speaker: Carla Louveira, Mozambique's Minister of Finance
a315.speech: Clarified that the domestic debt swap auctions held are provided for in the current public debt management strategy: “We have some BT [Treasury Bills] that were issued in the past, where their term was due to expire this year. It would be up to the government to decide whether to simply close them, pay them off or renew them. The strategy that is in force at the moment, until 2025, provides for what we call exchange auctions” ; insisted the auctions are part of the 2022-2025 strategy, to be reviewed by the new government for 2026-2029, and said “What we are doing in the current period is essentially what is already set out in the current approach,” with other measures to “rethink debt sustainability” to “be part of this revised strategy” through an “inclusive process” with the financial system and the central bank.

a315.speaker: Carla Louveira, Mozambique's Minister of Finance
a315.speech: “We are also working with our advisors on public debt (…), coming from the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, among other organisations that also provide support on matters relating to our country's debt.”

a315.speaker: Standard & Poor's (financial rating agency, ratings action)
a315.speech: Downgraded Mozambique's domestic public debt issues to selective default due to delays in payments to creditors and changes to a debt issue, describing Mozambique as having “exchanged Mozambican metical (MZN) 3.7 billion ($54 million) in local currency bonds maturing in March 2025 in return for longer-dated, lower-yielding bonds maturing in March 2030,” and noting that “the ongoing recourse to such liability management operations, coupled with a history of delayed payments on domestic debt, reflects the sovereign's constrained fiscal and liquidity positions” ; considers “this transaction distressed and tantamount to default” and says it has “therefore lowered our local currency rating on Mozambique to 'SD' (selective default) from 'CCC-'”.

a315.speaker: Standard & Poor's (financial rating agency)
a315.speech: Says it is maintaining the rating on foreign currency commercial debt obligations, not least because repayments “remain modest,” but warns that “potential delays to gas projects and foreign aid flows, alongside an uncertain external financing outlook, add to the pressures on Mozambique's finances.”

a315.speaker: Lusa (news agency report)
a315.speech: Reported on Monday that Standard & Poor's had downgraded Mozambique's domestic public debt issues to selective default.

a329.speaker: Statement signed by Zena Said, Chief Secretary (Katibu Mkuu Kiongozi)
a329.speech: Said the President of Zanzibar has appointed Fahad Soud Hamid as Executive Director of the People’s Bank of Zanzibar (PBZ), with the appointment taking effect on July 1, 2025. “Before this appointment, Fahad was Assistant Director, Finance Department, at the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), Tanzania,” part of the statement explained.

a400.speaker: President John Mahama, President of Ghana
a400.speech: In his inaugural address, stressed the importance of a robust public health system, acknowledging that epidemics threaten national stability.

a400.speaker: Auditor-General's report (Ghana)
a400.speech: Indicates that from March 2020 to June 2022, the government mobilized approximately GH¢21.8 billion to mitigate the pandemic's impact; however, nearly 50% of these funds were allocated for budgetary support rather than direct COVID-19 interventions.

a400.speaker: Public health experts
a400.speech: Have long emphasized the need for sustained investment in epidemic preparedness.

a400.speaker: Studies (on epidemic prevention cost-effectiveness)
a400.speech: Show that every dollar spent on epidemic prevention saves multiple times that amount in response and recovery costs.

a400.speaker: Harriet Nuamah Agyemang, Country Director of SEND Ghana
a400.speech: Urged the government to establish public health emergency funds at the local and national levels to better prepare the country for unforeseen health catastrophes; she believes the move is important as donor support for health emergencies continues to decline. “In recent times, we do not have donors wanting to give us as much as they used to or at all. We should begin to look within. That is the message of our advocacy since 2021, asking our government to use domestic resources to fund public health emergencies.”

a400.speaker: Harriet Nuamah Agyemang, Country Director of SEND Ghana
a400.speech: Further urged the Ministry of Health to incorporate a public health emergency fund into the revised Public Health Act: “We have called on the Ministry of Health to include a health emergency fund so that when the Act goes back to Parliament, the fund aspect will also be passed. That way, we will have a dedicated source of funding to implement the Public Health Act.”

a400.speaker: Rex Manu Yeboah, Deputy Director of the Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs
a400.speech: Acknowledged the importance of structured finance for public health emergencies, supporting the call for a legal framework to regulate financial allocations. He emphasized the importance of the government transitioning from an overreliance on donor-driven finance: “Our health sector has been largely donor-driven, and we have over-relied on external support to the extent that we are not able to organize ourselves to take care of it,” he said, adding, “With USAID funds now withdrawn, it is perhaps a blessing in disguise, pushing us to rethink and find innovative ways to mobilize internal revenue to fund public health emergencies.”

a400.speaker: Rex Manu Yeboah, Deputy Director of the Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs
a400.speech: Underlined that current legislation, such as the Local Government Act, Public Health and Sanitation Act, and NADMO Act, requires Metropolitan, Municipal, and District Assemblies (MMDAs) to allocate monies for health-related concerns; he pointed out that many assemblies have struggled to set aside finances for emergencies due to competing priorities and asked for a policy that necessitates a specific amount of the District Assemblies Common Fund (DACF) be committed to public health emergency preparedness ; “If we should have a fixed percentage of the Common Fund allocated for public health emergencies, it becomes a law that can be enforced. But currently, there is no such standardized percentage, and it is left to the discretion of the assemblies.”

a400.speaker: World Bank
a400.speech: Estimates that low- and middle-income countries could avoid billions in losses by investing in pandemic preparedness.

a436.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a436.speech: Announced on Wednesday 16 April the immediate disbursement of 129 million dollars, about 78.5 billion CFA francs, to support Mali in managing the consequences of the deadly floods of September and October 2024 ; according to the IMF, the floods caused significant damage to infrastructure, destroyed vast areas of farmland and undermined the livelihoods of thousands of families.

a436.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a436.speech: Foresees that the funds will also serve to strengthen the country's resilience to climate shocks, through the implementation of adaptation policies, improved early-warning systems and investment in sustainable infrastructure ; requires reforms in return for the aid.

a436.speaker: Malian authorities
a436.speech: Committed to strengthening tax administration and broadening the tax base, in order to increase State revenue and guarantee a lasting economic recovery.

a532.speaker: Guinness World Records (GWR), post on its official X handle
a532.speech: Confirmed that Nigerian chef Hilda Effiong Bassey (Hilda Baci) has set a new record by cooking the largest pot of Nigerian jollof rice: "New record: Largest serving of Nigerian style jollof rice - 8,780 kg (19,356 lb 9 oz) achieved by Hilda Baci and Gino in Victoria Island, Lagos, Nigeria."

a532.speaker: Hilda Effiong Bassey (Hilda Baci), Nigerian chef
a532.speech: Shared the exact breakdown of what went into the dish, which was cooked in a giant pot: 4,000 kg of washed basmati rice, making up at least 80% of the total weight, 164 kg of fresh goat meat, 220 kg of Gino Asun & peppered chicken cubes, and 600 kg of her own jollof pepper mix ; described the feat as the result of "nine hours of fire, passion and teamwork," noting that 1,200 kg of gas was used to prepare 16,600 plates of rice, which were "served with joy, love and community."

a545.speaker: Forbes estimates
a545.speech: Cited as the source that Mo Ibrahim earned somewhere between one and two billion dollars; also cited for the Forbes Africa Rich List, on which last year was the first time any women appeared, and for Patrice Motsepe's estimated fortune of $2.9 billion making him Africa's eighth-richest man.

a545.speaker: Patrice Motsepe, South African mining magnate
a545.speech: "Precious (his wife) and I will contribute at least half of the funds generated by our family assets to the Motsepe Foundation to be used during our lifetime and beyond to improve the lifestyles and living conditions of the poor, disabled, unemployed, women, youth, workers and marginalised South Africans, Africans and people around the world," said Motsepe in a "giving pledge" he made in January this year.

a545.speaker: Gideon Rachman, Financial Times
a545.speech: Observed: "Some argue that the founder's background in technology means that he is too transfixed by the search for technological 'magic bullets' to fix health problems, when often the problems involved are social or developmental: persuading Nigerian clerics to let children have the polio vaccine, persuading South African men to protect themselves better against HIV by getting circumcised."

a545.speaker: Aliko Dangote, Nigerian businessman and Africa's richest man
a545.speech: Announced that he is funding the construction of an $8 billion oil refinery in Nigeria: "This will really help not only Nigeria but sub-Saharan Africa. There has not been a new refinery for a long time in sub-Saharan Africa."

a545.speaker: Aliko Dangote, Nigerian billionaire
a545.speech: Told Reuters in an interview at his office in Lagos that he is targeting a market capitalisation of $35-40 billion for his cement company when he lists it in London next year, with the money to be used to pay off investors including himself, and said Dangote Cement had raised its capacity target to 60 million tonnes a year by 2015 from a previous 50 million tonne target.

a545.speaker: Daily Maverick commenters (correction note)
a545.speech: As some of our commenters noted, Patrice Motsepe did not actually pledge to give away half his fortune; instead, he pledged to "contribute at least half of the funds generated by our family assets".

a590.speaker: Elizabeth Tembo (not real name), HIV patient from Zingwangwa Township, Blantyre
a590.speech: "The day I went for my routine viral load check, I was told I can no longer do so because the services were suspended" ; said on Friday that the suspension means she will not know how her body is responding to treatment.

a590.speaker: A colleague of Elizabeth Tembo (anonymous HIV patient)
a590.speech: Said the situation is discouraging: "I also need to know if the treatment is working. It gives peace of mind to know."

a590.speaker: Analysis published on the Centre for Global Development website, by health researchers Pete Baker, Katherine Klemperer, Sam Hughes, Janeen Madan Keller and Javier Guzman
a590.speech: States that Malawi alongside 26 other countries will struggle to cover the US funding gap in the health sector; that the countries remain financially exposed and constrained, hence will not be able to fund their health sectors; it says between 2022 and 2023, Malawi received $228 million (K399 billion), representing 207 percent of the government's domestic health expenditure ; "These 26 countries-which collectively receive $3.4 billion in United States bilateral global health assistance can be considered as highly exposed, highly fiscally constrained and are exceptionally unlikely to be able to fill the [funding] gap" ; further states that the aid freeze is particularly concerning because other major global health donors, including European governments, are trimming their aid, which is resulting in low and middle-income countries facing mounting pressure; it says affected governments are yet to implement strategies to ensure healthcare provision in critical areas such as HIV continue ; "Governments have not yet developed the know-how, capacity to manage these kinds of services or procure these products because they are often managed by donors supra-nationally."

a590.speaker: Dr. Jobiba Chinkhumba, senior research associate (health economics), Malawi-Liverpool Wellcome Trust Clinical Research Programme and lecturer at Kamuzu University of Health Sciences
a590.speech: Said in an interview on Wednesday the aid freeze will have severe consequences and that to mitigate the adverse effects, government will need to re-prioritise and reallocate budgets to sustain essential services: "This will be a significant challenge for the country given the high burden of communicable, non-communicable diseases and competing demands for limited health sector resources. It is also crucial to ensure that every dollar in the health sector is used efficiently as the cost of wastage will be substantial" ; In the medium term, said government will have to explore domestic funding options for the health sector: "Efforts are already underway to expand the health financing sources with several reforms in progress. It is essential to accelerate the implementation of these reforms while carefully evaluating them to ensure sustainability and equitable contributions."

a590.speaker: Adrian Chikumbe, Ministry of Health spokesperson
a590.speech: Had not responded to our questionnaire as we went to press yesterday.

a590.speaker: US President Donald Trump
a590.speech: Issued an executive order on January 25 2025 freezing international aid.

a711.speaker: Prosper Ntahorwamiye, President of Burundi's Independent National Electoral Commission (CENI)
a711.speech: Said that CENI judged it appropriate to combine the CEPI and the CECI so that the members of these commissions would receive the same content at the same time and under the same conditions, and that these members would in turn train the polling-station members to be recruited shortly for the operationalisation of the electoral process; he indicated that overall, preparations for the 2025 elections are going well and are advancing properly. ; Stressed that to assign voters to polling stations, CENI has taken the figure of 500 voters as the reference figure for each polling station, with a special derogation for people who vote in places where they did not register, for example journalists, security agents accompanying the authorities, and observers; he added that in such cases the list must not exceed 25 voters at each polling station. ; Advised the members of these commissions to prepare well because the elections are very close; urged them to avoid favouritism in recruiting polling-station members, saying they must recruit those who are capable instead of considering existing affinities; and reminded them that well-prepared elections are the source of lasting peace, which is why they must work in the interest of the nation.

a745.speaker: Charles Kushner, US Ambassador to France
a745.speech: Described the move as a blow to peace, posting on his official X handle: "France's decision to recognise a Palestinian state is a gift to Hamas and a blow to peace. I've just arrived, and I'm deeply disappointed. @EmmanuelMacron - I hope to change your mind before September. Free the hostages. Focus on a ceasefire. This is the path to lasting peace."

a745.speaker: Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's Prime Minister
a745.speech: Condemned the move on his official X handle: "We strongly condemn President Macron's decision to recognise a Palestinian state next to Tel Aviv in the wake of the October 7 massacre. Such a move rewards terror and risks creating another Iranian proxy, just as Gaza became. A Palestinian state in these conditions would be a launch pad to annihilate Israel - not to live in peace beside it. Let's be clear: the Palestinians do not seek a state alongside Israel; they seek a state instead of Israel."

a745.speaker: Emmanuel Macron, French President
a745.speech: Announced via his official X handle that France will recognise the State of Palestine: "Consistent with its historic commitment to a just and lasting peace in the Middle East, I have decided that France will recognise the State of Palestine." ; "I will make this solemn announcement before the United Nations General Assembly this coming September." ; "The urgent priority today is to end the war in Gaza and to bring relief to the civilian population. We need an immediate ceasefire, the release of all hostages, and massive humanitarian aid for the people of Gaza. We must also ensure the demilitarization of Hamas, secure and rebuild Gaza." ; "And finally, we must build the State of Palestine, guarantee its viability, and ensure that by accepting its demilitarisation and fully recognising Israel, it contributes to the security of all in the region." ; "The French people want peace in the Middle East. It is our responsibility - as French citizens, alongside Israelis, Palestinians, and our European and international partners - to prove that peace is possible." ; "In light of the commitments made to me by the President of the Palestinian Authority, I have written to him to express my determination to move forward." ; "Trust, clarity, and resolve. We will achieve peace."

a1052.speaker: EU - Mozambique Political Dialogue (31st session, joint parties)
a1052.speech: Discussed the security situation in Europe, particularly the situation in Ukraine and the consequences of the war on global food security, and committed to continue working together and stand up for an international rules-based order and a peaceful world; the parties expressed their determination to continue to enhance bilateral partnership for mutual benefit and to develop synergies to face global challenges multilaterally.

a1052.speaker: Both delegations (Government of Mozambique and European Union)
a1052.speech: Highlighted the deep and long-standing friendship that connects both sides, based on common values and principles, and underlined the importance of dialogue to exchanging information, fostering mutual understanding and to facilitating priorities and common agendas.

a1052.speaker: EU delegation
a1052.speech: Saluted Mozambique for the election, for the first time, to join the UN Security Council as a non-permanent member.

a1052.speaker: EU and Member States delegation
a1052.speech: Made a presentation of the EU's global policies on development and security, namely the Global Gateway initiative and the Strategic Compass for Security and Defence, highlighting the global benefits and opportunities Mozambique can take advantage of in these two instruments; the EU also gave an overview of the new programming for assistance to Mozambique 2021-2027, whose priorities are Green Growth; Growth and Youth; and Governance, Peace and a Just Society.

a1069.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of Mozambique
a1069.speech: Sent his condolences to the Roman Catholic Church on the death of the Pope, recalling a spiritual leader with a "tireless commitment" to peace and social justice: "At this moment, with hearts in shock, we join the world in bidding farewell to a leader whose light shone brightly, illuminating paths of faith and hope" ; For Chapo, Pope Francis was a spiritual leader who fought for the marginalised, dedicating his life to a "tireless commitment" to justice, peace and fraternity ; "A pastor for all, he transcended the boundaries of the Roman Catholic Church, touching the soul of humanity with his message of love for God and neighbour. His voice, a true cry for justice, echoed in every corner of the planet, inspiring the building of bridges between cultures and religions."

a1069.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of Mozambique
a1069.speech: Recalled the Pope's visit to Mozambique in September 2019: "His apostolic visit to Mozambique in September 2019 remains a cherished moment in national historiography. Arriving in Maputo amid the challenges of post-cyclone recovery and tensions in Cabo Delgado, his presence was a powerful symbol of hope."

a1069.speaker: Pope Francis (homily at Mass in Maputo, September 2019)
a1069.speech: "Mozambique is a land of abundant natural and cultural riches, yet paradoxically, great numbers of its people live below the poverty level. And at times it seems that those who approach with the alleged desire to help have other interests. Sadly, this happens with brothers and sisters of the same land, who let themselves be corrupted. It is very dangerous to think that this is the price to be paid for foreign aid."

a1069.speaker: Vatican
a1069.speech: Said Pope Francis has died today aged 88, after 12 years of a pontificate marked by the fight against sexual abuse, wars and a pandemic.

a1405.speaker: Analysts at Absa Group
a1405.speech: According to analysts at Absa Group, South Africa looks set for much better growth in 2025 thanks to increased spending and investment, though a cooling of relations with the US may dim the outlook ; said on Tuesday that Africa's most industrialised economy could expand by 2.1% this year.

a1405.speaker: South African central bank (forecast)
a1405.speech: Forecast a 1.7% expansion, up from 0.7% in 2024.

a1450.speaker: Eyob Tekalign (PhD), State Minister for Finance of Ethiopia
a1450.speech: Outlined the content of his government's economic reform agenda, the "Homegrown Economic Reform Agenda," before representatives of the international community (members of the Development Assistance Group), acknowledging past accomplishments, soberly admitting "the limit to the road traveled to date" and rolling out the way forward.

a1450.speaker: Ricardo Hausmann, Center for International Development at Harvard University
a1450.speech: Equates the reform blueprint with "endodontic therapy" — a dental procedure where the doctor removes structures before subsequently cleaning, shaping and decontaminating the hollow with tiny files and irrigated solutions — based on his study of the bottlenecks of growth in Ethiopia.

a1450.speaker: Ethiopian government (official narrative)
a1450.speech: That there has been "fast and sustained growth" — a narrative the article says was not persuasive enough for a young population that continued to press with demands for more jobs and a response to income inequality among citizens and disparity between regional states.

a1507.speaker: Naomi Yohane, 37-year-old Cyclone Freddy survivor from Nkhulambe village
a1507.speech: "I still have dreams where I hear Blessings calling out for me," she says of her seven-year-old daughter, her voice calm but heavy.

a1507.speaker: Department of Disaster Management Affairs (Dodma) of Malawi
a1507.speech: has put the economic damage at over $500 million. ; Dodma says it's hard to measure the exact impact of the recent USAid funding pause.

a1507.speaker: Group village headman Nkhulambe
a1507.speech: says 187 of his fellow villagers perished. ; "We used to feed ourselves from the land," he says. "But now the fields are stone. Even with fertiliser, nothing grows. And then the fall armyworms came." ; "It's like nature turned against us," Nkhulambe adds.

a1507.speaker: Chipiliro Khamula, spokesperson for the Department of Disaster Management Affairs (Dodma)
a1507.speech: says the overall recovery strategy has been guided by a Post Disaster Needs Assessment, designed to mobilise resources and take action. "Save for the construction of the new Makhanga Primary School, relocation of affected communities, and rehabilitation of roads and health facilities, overall progress has been gradual due to inadequate funds," Khamula tells Dialogue Earth. "The total reconstruction and recovery needs for physical and economic losses caused by Freddy amount to $680.4 million – raising this substantial amount of funds has been a tall order." ; According to Khamula, over 15,000 households – most of them from flood-prone zones like Makhanga – have been relocated to safer, higher ground, a process involving clearing access roads, transporting families, and ensuring they had access to potable water.

a1507.speaker: Mary Likopa, 42-year-old widow and Cyclone Freddy survivor
a1507.speech: "The medicine costs three US dollars. We don't have it," she says of her grandson's untreated malaria. ; "No one from the government has come back since."

a1507.speaker: Pastor David Chigamba, representative of survivors in Chilobwe
a1507.speech: says the neglect is criminal. "They promised to relocate us. But nothing has happened. The land here should be declared a red zone. We are sitting in the path of death." ; "We live in fear," he says. "The government can fix this. They can reallocate land. They just choose not to."

a1507.speaker: Senior Dodma official (anonymous)
a1507.speech: admits that only 40 percent of the pledged funds have been disbursed. "Bureaucracy, capacity issues, and donor conditions are slowing us down," said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity. "But the frustration is real, and we understand that."

a1507.speaker: Hyoung-Joon Lim, WFP country director for Malawi
a1507.speech: says that after the cyclone WFP collaborated with Malawi's government to provide food assistance to over 550,000 people through "in-kind food and cash transfers." "We prioritised displaced families in camps and flood-affected communities. We focused on areas with the highest number of displaced people and the most severe infrastructure damage."

a1507.speaker: Hyoung-Joon Lim, WFP country director for Malawi
a1507.speech: On funding shortfalls: "WFP Malawi has experienced funding shortfalls that have affected the scale and timing of our operations," Lim says. "It may limit the number of people in need that we can reach." ; "We've had to make some very tough choices," Lim adds, on cutting food rations for refugees in Dzaleka Camp by 50% since July 2023 and pulling back on community and school feeding programmes.

a1507.speaker: Aid groups responding to Cyclone Freddy
a1507.speech: admit that key recovery efforts have stalled in the face of continued funding shortages.

a1562.speaker: Trump administration
a1562.speech: Justified the decision to shut down USAID by asserting that the agency no longer served the interests of the United States.

a1562.speaker: International study published in the medical journal The Lancet
a1562.speech: Reveals that the collapse of US funding for international aid could lead to more than 14 million additional deaths by 2030 among the most vulnerable populations, a third of them children.

a1562.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a1562.speech: Wrote: “On 1 July, USAID will officially cease to implement foreign assistance.” He specified that “foreign aid programmes that align with the administration's policies and that serve American interests will be administered by the State Department, where they will be implemented with greater accountability, strategy and efficiency.”

a1562.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a1562.speech: Criticised USAID's record, asserting that apart from creating a “global NGO industrial complex, USAID does not have much to show for itself since the end of the Cold War.”

a1562.speaker: George W. Bush and Barack Obama, former US presidents, and the singer Bono
a1562.speech: Paid tribute to USAID's work in a farewell message addressed to staff on Monday 30 June 2025.

a1562.speaker: Barack Obama, former US President
a1562.speech: Called the elimination of USAID “inexplicable” and a “colossal mistake” in a video seen by AFP.

a1562.speaker: George W. Bush, former US President
a1562.speech: Defended the PEPFAR programme against AIDS, which he had established through the agency.

a1726.speaker: The organisers of the Ibadan funfair (Oriyomi Hamzat, Queen Naomi Silekunola Ogunwusi and Abass Adetunji)
a1726.speech: Assured their fans that security was well taken care of.

a1726.speaker: Abba Moro, former Interior Minister and now Senator
a1726.speech: Picked this challenge while pleading his innocence in the 2014 stampede, and won with a resounding victory.

a1726.speaker: Unreliable sources (anonymous)
a1726.speech: Say the police might issue an international arrest warrant for His Eminence Pope Francis.

a1726.speaker: Youths queueing around the president's Bourdillon Drive residence in Lagos
a1726.speech: They claim they are there for monetary handouts.

a1726.speaker: President Bola Ahmed Tinubu
a1726.speech: Everywhere the president goes, he never forgets the slogan that under President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, Nigerians are richer than they think and better under him than they were under his revered predecessor, Muhammadu Buhari.

a2057.speaker: East African Legislative Assembly (EALA)
a2057.speech: Has passed a resolution urging the EAC Council of Ministers to fast-track the implementation of universal health insurance across all member states to ensure equitable access to quality healthcare ; also commended the EAC Council of Ministers for establishing the East African Health Research Commission (EAHRC) in Burundi.

a2057.speaker: Ambassador Fatma Ndangiza, Rwandan EALA Member
a2057.speech: Presenting the motion, commended Tanzania, Kenya and Rwanda for setting strong examples in promoting health insurance enrolment among their populations; said the resolution calls on the Council of Ministers and member states to accelerate universal health coverage by allocating at least 15 per cent of their national budgets to the health sector: “It is time to find sustainable solutions that reduce dependency on foreign aid and instead prioritise local investment to meet pressing needs, particularly in healthcare. Health must be recognised as a fundamental right for every citizen because health is wealth.”

a2057.speaker: Dr Gladbess Salema, EALA Member
a2057.speech: Said that achieving universal health coverage requires more than financial access, it also demands quality service delivery and efficient health systems.

a2057.speaker: Kanini Kega, Kenyan legislator (EALA)
a2057.speech: Observed that recent restrictions on foreign aid have exposed the region's vulnerabilities and urged EAC nations to strengthen domestic investment and engage the private sector to drive innovation and transformation in healthcare: “Uganda is a good example, having invested 6.1 per cent of its national budget in health, with ongoing efforts to increase funding and achieve self-sufficiency.”

a2365.speaker: Dr. Dorothy Gwajima, Tanzanian Minister for Community Development, Gender, Women, and Special Groups
a2365.speech: Announced during a press briefing in Dar es Salaam that President Samia Suluhu Hassan will be the chief guest at the national celebration of International Women's Day on March 8 in Arusha, and outlined key activities leading up to the event under the theme "Women and Girls: Strengthening Equality, Rights, and Empowerment."

a2365.speaker: Dr. Dorothy Gwajima, Tanzanian Minister for Community Development, Gender, Women, and Special Groups
a2365.speech: Noted that while International Women's Day is commemorated annually at regional levels, the national event is held every five years to evaluate progress in achieving gender equality and women's empowerment ; Said Arusha was selected to host this year's event as it has never held a national Women's Day celebration before ; Elaborated that a series of events have been planned ahead of the main celebration, saying the official launch will take place on March 1 at regional, district, and ward levels, bringing together women and stakeholders to assess progress and set future goals.

a2365.speaker: Dr. Dorothy Gwajima, Tanzanian Minister for Community Development, Gender, Women, and Special Groups
a2365.speech: Said the region, along with Manyara, also faces significant gender-related challenges, including high rates of female genital mutilation (FGM), with prevalence at 43 per cent and 28 per cent, respectively ; added that hosting the event in Arusha would help highlight these challenges and promote efforts to address them.

a2365.speaker: Dr. Dorothy Gwajima, Tanzanian Minister for Community Development, Gender, Women, and Special Groups
a2365.speech: Emphasized that this year's event carries special significance as it coincides with the 30th anniversary of the 1995 Beijing Declaration on gender equality, which Tanzania continues to implement as a UN member.

a2365.speaker: Dr. Dorothy Gwajima, Tanzanian Minister for Community Development, Gender, Women, and Special Groups
a2365.speech: Reflected on the history of International Women's Day, tracing its origins to 1911, when female industrial workers in the United States protested against poor working conditions and wage disparities.

a2393.speaker: Mozambican Government and the United States Embassy (joint public announcement)
a2393.speech: Publicly released on Monday in Maputo the 537 million dollar financing agreement under the second Compact of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC), stating that the money comes from the United States of America and will be used for the construction of climate-resilient infrastructure, coastal development and the strengthening of the local economies of Zambezia province that depend on agriculture and fisheries.

a2494.speaker: National Grid (UK system operator)
a2494.speech: "Our forecasts show electricity supply margins are expected to be tighter than normal on Monday evening. These are precautionary measures to maintain the buffer of spare capacity."

a2494.speaker: Maxar Technologies
a2494.speech: Forecast that London will be as cold as minus 2C on Monday.

a2494.speaker: Grid data
a2494.speech: Show consumption is expected to peak on Monday evening at 44.7 gigawatts, up from 42.2 gigawatts on Sunday.

a2494.speaker: Jeremy Hunt, Chancellor of the Exchequer
a2494.speech: Pledged £6 billion (R127 billion) to insulate homes and upgrade boilers in his budget last year.

a2603.speaker: Daud Mohamed Omar, Puntland’s Minister of Planning
a2603.speech: “This is an important meeting. Our discussions focused on how Puntland can become more self-sufficient.”

a2603.speaker: Said Jama Qorshel, Puntland Minister of Health
a2603.speech: Echoed the call for local businesspeople and investors to contribute financially to the health sector, aiming to make healthcare more affordable and accessible.

a2603.speaker: Puntland officials (at the health investment conference)
a2603.speech: Proposed several strategies to boost domestic revenue for health services, including imposing a special fee on products and services that pose health risks—such as khat, tobacco, and cosmetics—launching a phased community health insurance system starting with government employees, establishing a healthcare cost-sharing system, and encouraging direct private investment through Public-Private Partnership (PPP) initiatives and Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) programs.

a2603.speaker: Dr. Fadumo Hosh, university lecturer
a2603.speech: Emphasized the urgency of developing local solutions, saying: “The shock of the aid cut was significant. What matters now is whether a real plan will be developed and implemented.”

a2603.speaker: Mohamed Hassan, Puntland Civil Society Network
a2603.speech: Acknowledged the severe impact of the funding cuts but remained hopeful: “There is a possibility to find local solutions. This conference represents a promising step toward cost-sharing between the government and civil society.”

a2603.speaker: Yasin Jama, Member of Parliament
a2603.speech: Stressed the importance of continued collaboration: “We are seeing more willingness from civil society, but the government must also step up its efforts.”

a2603.speaker: United States Agency for International Development (USAID) figures
a2603.speech: In fiscal year 2023, USAID allocated approximately $1.05 billion in foreign assistance to Somalia, supporting humanitarian relief, health services, education, governance, and infrastructure development; by fiscal year 2024, USAID’s humanitarian assistance to Somalia had dropped to approximately $116 million.

a2626.speaker: Eugène Assédé, head of the palm oil production improvement project (NGO Sassimecc Group)
a2626.speech: Said that before the implementation of the project, palm oil production at the 10 sites was carried out by artisanal methods with makeshift equipment, and that for a whole season the network produces only about 12,000 litres of oil; said the acquisition of equipment financed by MCA-Benin gives a boost to the functioning of the sites and allows beneficiaries to realise that it is possible to escape poverty by improving the artisanal production system; listed the equipment acquired (2 motorised crushers, 2 motorised presses, 2 motorised defibrators, 2 motorised stripping machines, 3 cookers, 2 manual winnowers, 2 large-mesh and 2 small-mesh sorters, 2 clarifiers, 10 motorcycles, 50 palm seedlings and 50 merinda seedlings); went on to say that other activities are under way, such as the acquisition of generators and 4 training sessions that will soon be organised.

a2626.speaker: MCA-Benin delegation
a2626.speech: Very satisfied with everything that has been undertaken, promised to continue along the same lines in order to achieve the objectives of the programme.

a2626.speaker: Nicolas Ahouandjinou, head of the Gatid Consortium
a2626.speech: Explained to the delegation how the production chain works, saying the Consortium is made up of three entities: Detaren, an agri-food company specialising in essential oils from therapeutic and aromatic plants and flavoured water called “Eau Noble”; GEA-Benin, an umbrella producers’ organisation which defends its members’ interests, supports their organisational development and capacity-building and develops agricultural value chains, and within which the aromatic plants sector is supported; and FMB-Group, specialising in the design and manufacture of agri-food processing equipment, in which several research works and inventions are recognised.

a2626.speaker: Nicolas Ahouandjinou, head of the Gatid Consortium
a2626.speech: Specified that thanks to this financial support several sectors have been strengthened — for Detaren most contracts have been signed, production equipment and the stock of essential oils delivered; for GEA-Benin the young aromatic seedlings have been delivered and the motor pump contract signed; for FMB-Group the contracts are signed and complementary machine tools ordered, awaiting receipt in the coming weeks for installation; said this support constitutes a decisive lever for the Consortium: “A sustainable agricultural value chain will come into being to impact 20,000 actors within 2 years thanks to the support of MCA-Benin.”

a2626.speaker: Soulé Issa Badarou, Minister and chairman of the board of directors of MCA-Benin
a2626.speech: Very satisfied, did not fail to point out that this is a first in the sub-region that deserves to be encouraged and supported.

a2628.speaker: Finance.yahoo.com (data)
a2628.speech: Documents the ownership of Diageo, listing the top institutional holders of the stock as Bank of America Corporation, FMR LLC, Morgan Stanley and ClearBridge Investments LLC.

a2628.speaker: Records (historical)
a2628.speech: According to records, Diageo’s story did not begin until 1997 when Guinness merged with the food and beverage wholesaler Grand Metropolitan Plc; the $15.8 billion deal went smoothly, and the two companies merged under the Diageo name.

a2650.speaker: Kagiso Molatlhwa, Executive Director of Botswana Council of Non-Governmental Organisations (BOCONGO)
a2650.speech: Has highlighted the urgent need for sustainable funding mechanisms and emphasised that the private sector plays a crucial role in supporting NGOs but requires incentives to enhance their contributions. “This comes after dwindling donor funds and the US cutting foreign aid,” she said in an interview. ; “While some private sector entities recognise the valuable role that NGOs play in national development and have corporate social investment (CSI) initiatives in place, there is a need for long-term and sustainable investment.” ; Explained that many private sector entities already support NGOs through foundations, capacity-building initiatives, technical expertise, and donations targeting key development areas such as health, education, child protection, and ICT. However, she added, sustained investment is necessary to ensure NGOs continue making a meaningful impact.

a2650.speaker: Kagiso Molatlhwa, Executive Director of BOCONGO
a2650.speech: “The private sector has been as supportive as possible, but many companies want recognition for their contributions and a return on investment,” Molatlhwa stated. ; “Visibility is also a key factor, as it helps market their services while simultaneously promoting social good.”

a2650.speaker: Private sector stakeholders / companies (feedback reported)
a2650.speech: Feedback from the private sector indicates that while companies are willing to support civil society organisations (CSOs), they often seek policy and legal reforms to provide more tangible benefits for their contributions. Stakeholders in the private sector have expressed interest in incentives such as tax breaks and rebates, which they believe would encourage more businesses to invest in social development programmes.

a2650.speaker: BOCONGO (organisational position)
a2650.speech: According to BOCONGO, government intervention in the form of tax incentives and other supportive policies would not only enhance private sector engagement but would also secure the long-term sustainability of NGOs. This, in turn, would ensure that civil society continues to contribute meaningfully to Botswana’s national development agenda.

a2650.speaker: NGOs driving key government programmes (recently released report)
a2650.speech: Have raised alarm over their worsening financial situation, warning that many are teetering on the edge of collapse. In a recently released report, they revealed that severe funding shortages and sustainability challenges have already forced some to shut down while many others are struggling to stay afloat. The crisis, they say, threatens to derail critical social and developmental initiatives, raising concerns about the long-term viability of these organisations and their ability to support national priorities.

a2753.speaker: International Republican Institute (IRI) preliminary statement
a2753.speech: Released its preliminary statement on Mozambique's October 9, 2024 general election, producing key findings and 11 recommendations. Key findings: the electoral process has so far fallen short of international standards for democratic elections, with delayed accreditation of party agents and observers, FRELIMO disproportionately benefiting from the use of state resources, inflated voter rolls exceeding population estimates particularly in FRELIMO strongholds, inconsistent security and voter intimidation in Zambezia, Niassa and Sofala, limited transparency in result collation and publication, late electoral law changes published less than seven weeks before election day, vote buying and intimidation of opposition parties, and 13 critical incidents recorded including ballot stuffing and restricted access for observers. Recommendations include strengthening CNE budgetary independence, publishing electoral law amendments well in advance, enforcing prohibitions on state resource misuse, reducing counting time to less than 15 days, publishing results in open-data format, ensuring timely accreditation, transparent procurement, a permanent voter register, allowing voters to confirm registration, and promoting inclusive participation of vulnerable groups and women. IRI urges authorities to ensure a fair, transparent, accurate and peaceful count, and calls on the CNE and the Government of Mozambique to conduct a timely and credible count; IRI expresses its gratitude to the people of Mozambique.

a2753.speaker: Dr. Succès Masra, former Prime Minister of Chad and head of the IRI International Election Observation Mission
a2753.speech: “Despite challenges, the democratic spirit of the Mozambican people is strong. Mozambican citizens were not deterred from exercising their right to determine their future,” said Masra. “Vibrant democracies require that citizens elect their leaders through a competitive, open, inclusive, and transparent process.”

a2753.speaker: International Republican Institute (@IRIglobal, social media post)
a2753.speech: “#MOZAMBIQUE ELECTION: ‘Despite challenges, the democratic spirit of the Mozambican people is strong.’ In a preliminary statement, IRI commends voters' commitment to democracy, but finds the electoral process fell short of international standards.”

a2858.speaker: Dawit Wondimagegn (MD), associate professor of psychiatry at Addis Abeba University’s School of Medicine and chief executive director of Tikur Anbessa Hospital (opinion article)
a2858.speech: Writes that the relatively milder trajectory of the COVID-19 pandemic in Africa may create a pseudo sense of safety and protection among both the populace and African governments, and that, combined with the severity of the damage the virus is causing the rich world, there is a possibility that Africa may be left behind in the scramble for COVID-19 vaccines ; argues that the US remains the single most important actor in saving millions of lives through the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) and that Africa is indebted to the US for its generosity for bringing the region back from the edge of collapse ; urges that what governments and citizens of developing countries could and should do now is focus on hammering on the good public health prevention methods that are tested and proven.

a2858.speaker: Angela Merkel, German Chancellor
a2858.speech: Expressed concern about not leaving developing countries behind, after the recent G20 meeting which tangentially promised equitable access and distribution of vaccines to emerging countries.

a2969.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a2969.speech: Has called for new governance, business, and financing models to achieve sustainable health financing and development across the world; he said the prevailing global development architecture was no longer fit for purpose; that global health crises, especially in Africa, were not only issues of diseases, vaccines and hospitals, but also social and economic inequality, symptoms of deeper malaise in the global development architecture itself; he added that the traditional aid system had collapsed, with developing countries struggling with punishing debt burdens and fragmented supply chains ; “Developing countries now spend more on servicing external debts than they do on health care and education combined. Africa's external debt stock alone exceeded $1 trillion in 2023, with debt service consuming nearly one-fifth of government revenues in many African countries.”

a2969.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a2969.speech: Said “Accra Reset”, a new global governance for health and development, had proposed a new development paradigm that prioritises health sovereignty, economic resilience, and global solidarity ; “We need to strategise. The world needs a reset, a reengineering of the very logic of development itself. This is the vision of the Accra Reset, to rebuild global development around sovereignty, workability and shared value, to make it possible to co-invest, co-design and co-create for shared priorities.”

a2969.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a2969.speech: Further said there had been some achievements made over the last two decades, where millions of people were taken out of poverty, as well as maternal mortality declining by a third since 2000, coupled with expanded access to vaccines, HIV treatment and malaria prevention; he, however, said the progress was erased by the COVID-19 pandemic in less than two years, turning back the clock ; “The COVID-19 pandemic erased two decades of poverty reduction in less than two years. Climate change has driven nearly 735 million people back into chronic hunger. Almost one in 10 of the world's population is facing chronic hunger.”

a2969.speaker: Olusegun Obasanjo, former President of Nigeria
a2969.speech: Emphasised the need for global solidarity in addressing health issues, particularly in developing countries; he mentioned climate change, pandemics, and financial contagion as some of the issues that needed to be addressed; Mr Obasanjo said solidarity was not charity, but a common security and insurance policy for all nations ; “Through the Jubilee 2000 campaign, over $100 billion in debt for more than 30 African countries was cancelled. The launch of the Global Fund to Fight AIDS raised over $50 billion and saved millions of lives in the late 1990s and early 2000s. That was not an act of charity; it was an act of solidarity and justice.”

a2969.speaker: UN 2023 Report
a2969.speech: Indicated that fewer than half of the 169 SDG targets were on track, while on health, the situation was particularly dire with inequality and fiscal resilience, especially as official development assistance was reported to be in decline by some 40 per cent.

a3195.speaker: Selibe Mochoboroane, Minister of Health of Lesotho
a3195.speech: Said in an exclusive interview with the Lesotho Times that the Ministry of Health will next week sign an agreement with the United States government to pilot the newly developed HIV prevention drug lenacapavir, and that the agreement marked renewed US commitment to supporting Lesotho's HIV response, following a period of reduced funding ; “Recently, I visited the United States where I met with government representatives. Among the key issues discussed was Lesotho piloting the administration of lenacapavir” ; “We agreed that the US government will introduce this kind of vaccine. The US also proposes the ‘America First Global Health Strategy,’ which is built on three pillars — making America safe, great, and prosperous.”

a3195.speaker: Selibe Mochoboroane, Minister of Health of Lesotho
a3195.speech: Explained that the “make America safe” pillar includes helping countries like Lesotho to prevent infectious diseases to reduce global health risks, but that continued US assistance is conditional on countries' performance in previous aid programmes such as PEPFAR.

a3195.speaker: Selibe Mochoboroane, Minister of Health of Lesotho
a3195.speech: Said Lesotho's outstanding progress in the HIV response has strengthened its eligibility for inclusion in the lenacapavir pilot ; “Globally, the HIV target is 95-95-95 by 2030 — meaning 95% of people living with HIV should know their status, 95% of those who know their status should be on treatment, and 95% of those on treatment should have suppressed viral loads” ; “We have surpassed these global targets. Lesotho is at 97-97-99” ; He added that by 2030, countries are also expected to reduce new HIV infections by 90%, and Lesotho currently stands at 87%.

a3195.speaker: Selibe Mochoboroane, Minister of Health of Lesotho
a3195.speech: Said Lesotho's strong tuberculosis (TB) response was another factor in its selection for the lenacapavir pilot: “Global targets require countries to reduce the TB burden by 90% by 2030. Lesotho is on track, increasing TB notifications and ensuring patients receive treatment. This puts us in a strong position — among the 16 countries selected by the US government to continue working with.”

a3195.speaker: Selibe Mochoboroane, Minister of Health of Lesotho
a3195.speech: Added that the US will also assist Lesotho in strengthening human resources for health, particularly by increasing the number of frontline healthcare workers: “I have received a letter from the US government informing me that their delegation will arrive in Lesotho in the first week of November to negotiate and sign the new deal.”

a3195.speaker: US Department of State (statement)
a3195.speech: Announced in August 2025 plans to make lenacapavir available in countries with high HIV burdens, including Lesotho, describing it as a highly effective HIV prevention medication that requires administration only twice a year, with the rollout prioritising pregnant and breastfeeding women who face a higher risk of HIV transmission, and aiming to reach up to two million people by 2028 ; “In the coming months, PEPFAR will collaborate with partner countries to develop detailed rollout strategies, prioritising high-risk groups — especially mothers and infants.”

a3195.speaker: Large-scale clinical trial of lenacapavir
a3195.speech: Demonstrated remarkable results, with over 99% of participants remaining HIV-negative while on lenacapavir.

a3195.speaker: Jeremy Lewis, US Senior Official for Foreign Assistance, Humanitarian Affairs and Religious Freedom
a3195.speech: Said lenacapavir's twice-yearly dosage offers major advantages: “The dosage schedule increases convenience and adherence, helping reduce transmission rates and lower treatment costs” ; “The US will continue partnering with countries with large HIV epidemics to co-develop targeted distribution plans, with a strong emphasis on preventing mother-to-child transmission.”

a3195.speaker: Peter Sands, Global Fund Executive Director
a3195.speech: Emphasised the importance of fast-tracking access to medical innovations like lenacapavir: “We must ensure breakthrough tools are introduced quickly, affordably, and where they will have the greatest impact” ; “By focusing on regions where lenacapavir can make the biggest difference — and working closely with the US and Gilead — we can help countries integrate this innovation into their HIV prevention programmes. This will reduce new infections and accelerate progress toward self-reliance and epidemic control.”

a3223.speaker: United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF)
a3223.speech: Has called on the government at all levels to reduce reliance on external sources for health funding and instead make adequate provisions in their budgets.

a3223.speaker: Rowan Khan, UNICEF Deputy Representative in Nigeria
a3223.speech: Made the statement on Wednesday in Abuja at the Primary Health Care (PHC) Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) Learning and Dissemination Event; according to Ms Khan, the US administration's pause of foreign aid, affecting nearly all its foreign aid programmes, is no surprise but a wake-up call to stop reliance on external funding for health: "Looking at what is happening at the global level, we need to really reduce the reliance on others at all levels. What has happened with the U.S. government's decision has shaken us to the core, but honestly, we knew this was coming because we cannot forever rely on external support. All of us need to have our own ownership, our own accountabilities, and our own responsibilities as well."

a3223.speaker: Rowan Khan, UNICEF Deputy Representative in Nigeria
a3223.speech: Emphasised the importance of coordination among stakeholders and optimizing available resources, considering the limitations in both financial and human resources, and added that such efforts would have a more significant impact on Nigeria's future; suggested that state governments should conduct a proper budget analysis focused on identifying gaps, particularly regarding basic services for children and the revitalisation of PHCs in each ward: "So, I urge all state authorities to look at this very carefully. Please look at your budgets and see how we can intuitively allocate resources for the basic services of health, specifically for immunisation and other basic services."

a3223.speaker: Manasseh Jatau, Deputy Governor of Gombe State
a3223.speech: Stressed the importance of Nigeria beginning to sponsor research to produce medicines and vaccines from local plants; explained that Nigeria had sufficient plant resources to produce vaccines, which could reduce the cost of vaccine importation: "We must take responsibility for our health issues. My dear governors and medical personnel, we are challenged to take responsibility for obvious reasons. In the long run, we should be prepared in case there's donor doubt, donor denial, donor fatigue, and eventually donor stoppage. If we don't get ready for that, a calamity is waiting for us."

a3223.speaker: Jesicca Crawford, Country Manager of GAVI
a3223.speech: Commended the governors of the implementing states for their commitment to the programme; said such commitment was necessary to build a healthier, more resilient Nigeria, where every child, citizen, and woman had access to quality PHC services; urged the governors to ensure that the services were sustained and that the achievements made through the MoU were replicated in other states.

a3223.speaker: Mya Ngon, team lead for Communicable and Non-Communicable Diseases at the World Health Organisation (WHO)
a3223.speech: Acknowledged the successes recorded but stressed the need for further work to reduce zero-dose immunisation among unimmunised children: "We also need to sustain government efforts to implement PHC strengthening and immunisation to improve equitable access to vaccines and reduce zero-dose children. We should remember our national goal to invest in reducing reliance on campaigns and focus more on strengthening the health system."

a3223.speaker: Halima Muhammed, Senior Programme Manager for Immunisation at the Nigeria Governors Forum (NGF)
a3223.speech: Noted that the MoU had significantly strengthened PHC systems over the past three years, ensuring that many children received vaccines: "The NGF, alongside our esteemed partners, has played a pivotal role in implementing targeted interventions. These efforts have enhanced service delivery, increased demand generation, strengthened disease surveillance, improved governance, optimised human resources, fortified supply chains, and driven high-level advocacy to ensure sustained political commitment to PHC" ; also highlighted the importance of sustaining these gains through the Sector-Wide Approach (SWAp) programme by integrating resources, policies, and initiatives across the health sector.

a3223.speaker: News Agency of Nigeria (NAN)
a3223.speech: Reports that the PHC MoU Health Systems Strengthening Initiative is a three-year partnership (2022 to March 2025) between GAVI, the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, and UNICEF; NAN reports that to ensure sustainability, the initiative is transitioning programme ownership to state governments.

a3500.speaker: Mano River Institute for Strategic Studies (MRISS)
a3500.speech: Has been closely monitoring the response of the Mano River Union (MRU) countries to the recent suspension of USAID assistance; said that while the aid suspension has presented significant challenges to the region's development agenda, it has also created opportunities for the MRU countries to diversify their funding sources and promote self-reliance.

a3500.speaker: Mano River Institute for Strategic Studies (MRISS)
a3500.speech: Makes the following recommendations: 1. Strengthen domestic resource mobilization, including increasing tax revenue, improving public financial management, and leveraging private sector investment; 2. Promote private sector development, including investing in infrastructure, promoting access to finance, and developing the skills of the workforce; 3. Foster regional integration by strengthening regional institutions and promoting trade and economic cooperation; 4. Develop a regional development plan outlining priorities and strategies for promoting economic development and reducing poverty; 5. Engage with international partners to explore alternative funding opportunities and to leverage technical assistance and expertise. MRISS will continue to monitor the MRU countries' response to the aid suspension and provide policy recommendations to support their efforts to promote self-reliance and sustainable development.

a3798.speaker: OECD
a3798.speech: According to the OECD, over $51 billion in official development assistance flowed into Africa in 2022.

a3798.speaker: UNESCO
a3798.speech: According to UNESCO, technical and vocational enrolment in Ethiopia increased by over 450% between 2000 and 2020, illustrating the transformative power of education that equips youth to create rather than wait.

a3798.speaker: The African Development Bank, the African Union, and the IMF, among others
a3798.speech: Estimate that corruption drains over $100 billion from the continent each year; funds that could be used to construct schools, roads, hospitals, and foster hope.

a3798.speaker: African Development Bank
a3798.speech: According to the African Development Bank, of the nearly 420 million youth aged 15 to 35, one-third are unemployed and discouraged, another one-third are vulnerably employed, and only one in six is in wage employment.

a3799.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a3799.speech: Has called on African nations to become more self-reliant following the withdrawal of funding support from the United States Agency for International Development (USAID); describing the development as "adversity in opportunity," stressed the need for African countries to strengthen their economic resilience and reduce dependence on foreign aid.

a3799.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a3799.speech: Revealed that he had directed the Minister of Finance to adjust the national budget to compensate for the shortfall caused by USAID's withdrawal: "This amounts to $156 million for 2025, which is a bit above GH2 billion" ; assured that the government would make the necessary budgetary adjustments: "Happily, when we have elections, we don't present the budget until the new government takes over. And so, we're supposed to present the budget in March, so it's possible for us to make provision to cover what the shortfall in US assistance is going to be."

a3799.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a3799.speech: Said the USAID funding supported four critical areas of Ghana's economy - governance and democracy, healthcare, economic growth, and education - and highlighted healthcare as the most affected sector, particularly maternal care and the US President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR): "The biggest chunk of it was about $78 million, which went into maternities, PEPFAR activities, HIV testing, provision of antiretrovirals, and other healthcare support."

a3799.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a3799.speech: Acknowledged the evolving geopolitical landscape, noting that while the US had played a vital role in shaping the post-world order, its current recalibration was disruptive: "The US has prospered from the post-world order. But it has gotten to a stage where it wants to recalibrate, and it has a right to recalibrate. But I believe that the recalibration should be in a less disruptive manner than it is happening now." ; warned that the US could lose its influence by pulling away from global assistance programs: "One of the things that the US is going to lose is that soft power that it has wielded in the world. People are grateful for the kind of assistance that they get. And so, for the US to decide that, no, we don't want to have anything to do with it anymore, then they lose some of that soft power."

a3799.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a3799.speech: Remained optimistic about Africa's ability to forge new partnerships: "And that's why we have a multipolar world. We are no longer a unipolar world. And so, as bridges are burning, new bridges are being formed, and we need to look for those new bridges and be able to link the world to those new bridges."

a3799.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a3799.speech: Underscored the withdrawal of USAID funding as a wake-up call for Africa to become more self-sufficient, particularly in protecting vulnerable communities: "We should roll out more safety nets. We must go for more equitable societies, bridge the gap between the rich and the poor, and put out opportunities for our young people to be able to make a life for themselves."

a3799.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a3799.speech: Pointed to progress in continental trade as a sign of Africa's growing economic independence, highlighting the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Agreement (AfCFTA): "We're able to export tariff-free into our countries. Of course, there are obstacles because our trade channels have been the colonial trade channels between us and Europe and not amongst ourselves" ; stressed the need to improve intra-African infrastructure to facilitate trade and economic cooperation.

a3799.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a3799.speech: Expressed confidence in Africa's potential, citing the continent's youthful population and innovative spirit as key drivers of future growth: "But I do believe, as a student of psychology, that in all adversities there is opportunity, and new orders bring out of disruptions." ; "The disruption that is taking place now is going to yield a new order because we will have to adapt to what is happening."

a4028.speaker: Reports from Argentina
a4028.speech: Claim that Messi wants to go and play in a league with genuine competition before the 2026 World Cup finals, which will be held in the United States, arrive; he is claimed to be considering a loan transfer to a fiercely competitive league in order to get himself ready to lead Argentina’s efforts to defend the World Cup title next year.

a4028.speaker: Mark Hughes, former Manchester City coach
a4028.speech: Claimed that the owner of that team, Sheikh Mansour, tried to sign Messi when he bought the Etihad club.

a4028.speaker: Guillem Balague, Spanish journalist
a4028.speech: Believes a return to Barcelona has little likelihood of happening because of the bad relationship existing between Messi and the club’s president, Joan Laporta.

a4028.speaker: Fans (unnamed)
a4028.speech: Claimed that Messi wanted to punch his former teammate, Vitinha, during the Club World Cup round-of-16 match.

a4078.speaker: Isman Ibrahim Robleh, Djiboutian Minister of Labour in charge of administrative reform
a4078.speech: During the discussions, also raised with his counterparts several other areas of collaboration between his department and American international development actors.

a4078.speaker: Djibouti's Ministry of Labour and the USAID delegation (joint position)
a4078.speech: At the end of the meeting, the two parties reaffirmed their firm intention to collaborate and to coordinate their efforts in order to give new impetus to their partnership.

a4176.speaker: Gilles Carbonnier, International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) vice-president
a4176.speech: Told AFP that Africa accounts for roughly 40 per cent of the world’s armed conflicts, with some 50 ongoing clashes across the continent ; “We now have more than 50 active armed conflict situations in Africa” ; said this represents a 45 per cent increase since 2020, and accounts for “approximately 40 per cent of total conflicts in the world” ; “The humanitarian consequences are truly dramatic, because we have some 35 million people displaced due to these conflicts in African countries, and this represents almost half of the displaced people in the world.”

a4176.speaker: Gilles Carbonnier, ICRC vice-president
a4176.speech: Said the ICRC, like many other humanitarian organisations, faces a decline in funding due to massive aid cuts by the United States and other Western countries this year – despite the “enormous” needs ; “These force us to make very painful choices, where we must reduce, or even cease, some of our operations to prioritise others.”

a4176.speaker: Gilles Carbonnier, ICRC vice-president
a4176.speech: Said the most “worrying” situation is Sudan, gripped by a civil war since April 2023 ; “We have a health system that is largely destroyed”, with the ICRC worried about the resurgence of cholera, malaria and dengue fever.

a4176.speaker: Gilles Carbonnier, ICRC vice-president
a4176.speech: Condemned the resurgence of fighting in Somalia, a Horn of Africa country still battling the militant Al-Shabaab group, and in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, where violence has intensified since January with the capture of the major cities of Goma and Bukavu by the Kigali-backed M23 armed group.

a4176.speaker: International study published in July
a4176.speech: Revealed that the withdrawal of US aid could lead to more than 14 million additional deaths by 2030 among the most vulnerable, a third of them children.

a4176.speaker: United Nations
a4176.speech: Calls the situation in Sudan “the world’s worst humanitarian crisis.”

a4481.speaker: International Court of Justice (ICJ) (communique)
a4481.speech: Declared in a communique that it will issue its decision on Friday at 15:00 Hague time (14:00 in Lisbon) on South Africa's request for the "modification and indication of provisional measures".

a4481.speaker: South Africa (Pretoria), in its request to the ICJ
a4481.speech: Argued, on 10 May, that the previous provisional measures required by the court, following its first request, "were not able to fully respond to the change in circumstances and to the new facts", given the offensive in Rafah, and requested "additional measures and the revision of the previous ones" ; Stated that the Israeli authorities had shown contempt for the ICJ by "ignoring and violating" the provisional measures issued in January and March, after the court had ordered the country to "take all possible measures" to prevent a genocide in the enclave.

a4481.speaker: Oren Marmorstein, spokesman for the Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs
a4481.speech: Accused Pretoria of acting as an arm of Hamas and of "distorting reality", reiterating that the Army "acts in accordance with international law and humanitarian obligations".

a4481.speaker: Hamas (Islamic Resistance Movement)
a4481.speech: Announced that it accepted a ceasefire proposal presented by Egypt and Qatar, which the Israeli authorities considered insufficient.

a4481.speaker: United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA)
a4481.speech: According to UNRWA, around 900,000 people have fled the city of Rafah.

a4481.speaker: Gaza authorities, controlled by Hamas
a4481.speech: According to the Gaza authorities, Israeli attacks have already caused the deaths of more than 35,700 Palestinians, to which are added more than 510 Palestinians killed in the West Bank and East Jerusalem by Israeli forces and in settler attacks since 7 October of last year.

a4574.speaker: Manoma Vusie Masango, National Commissioner of Police (Royal Eswatini Police Service)
a4574.speech: Called on 32 Individual Police Officers to embody discipline, honour, and respect for human rights as they prepare to join AUSSOM in Mogadishu, and reminded the officers that their role is not only to represent Eswatini but also to safeguard civilians and uphold international law in a conflict-torn region. "You have reflected an earnest intention on the commitment of member states to the contribution of peace and security in the continent," Masango said. "Go with purpose, humility, and the unwavering determination to serve the African people. Your safety, conduct, and discipline will remain our highest priority and concern." ; Emphasized the importance of adhering to International Humanitarian Law and International Human Rights Law while on mission, stressing that the officers must protect civilians and respect the Rule of Law in line with the principles of African Union Peace Support Operations.

a4574.speaker: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a4574.speech: According to OCHA, over 6.9 million Somalis currently need humanitarian assistance due to conflict, drought, and food insecurity.

a4574.speaker: The African Union and its international partners, including the United Nations and the European Union
a4574.speech: Have repeatedly stressed that instability in Somalia is a continental concern.

a4574.speaker: African Union
a4574.speech: Has committed to a gradual transfer of security responsibilities to Somali authorities, with the ultimate goal of allowing Somalia to take full ownership of its peace and security.

a4634.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a4634.speech: Announced plans to reopen discussions with the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) for the release of a US$190 million grant to support reforms in Ghana's electricity distribution sector; highlighted the critical state of Ghana's energy sector, describing it as the "Achilles heel" of the nation's financial and economic stability. "I spoke to the Americans during my last visit to the US.
