And it needs to be able to cope with multidimensional and complex challenges, including a growing population and climate change.”

a7053.speaker: Meshack Malo, FAO Country Representative
a7053.speech: Said the Aweil Rice Scheme’s resilience to climate-related disasters highlights the scheme’s possibility of overcoming environmental obstacles with the right investments. “The Aweil Rice Scheme has great potential, and its transformation into an irrigation scheme will further improve productivity. Private sector engagement is crucial, as progressive farmers are already playing a role in expanding agricultural production,” Malo emphasized.

a7053.speaker: Humanitarian Community (projection)
a7053.speech: Last year projected that 9.3 million people – 69 per cent of South Sudan’s total population of 13.4 million – would require some form of humanitarian assistance in 2025.

a7053.speaker: Body of relief agencies (2025 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan)
a7053.speech: While launching the 2025 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP), appealed for US$1.7 billion to provide life-saving assistance to 5.4 million people experiencing the most acute needs.

a7053.speaker: High-level panel on food systems
a7053.speech: According to the high-level panel, for South Sudan’s food system to thrive, clear government policies and increased investment in agriculture are needed.

a7053.speaker: Dr. Tony Ngalamu, Associate Professor at the University of Juba
a7053.speech: Stressed the importance of policies that support farmers, improve market access, and encourage private sector engagement to drive sustainable food production. “National food systems pathways are essential for advancing food security. To achieve meaningful progress, we need to focus on three key priorities: securing finance, ensuring peace, and strengthening the interface between agricultural systems. Farmers must be at the center of these interventions,” said Dr. Ngalamu.

a7053.speaker: Hon. Dr. John Kanisio, Undersecretary and National Convener for food systems at the Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security
a7053.speech: Reiterated that South Sudan has the capacity to feed itself. “But we must strengthen our local food production systems. Relying on imports and food aid is not a long-term solution. Investing in local farmers and agribusinesses will create jobs and improve food security,” he added.

a7053.speaker: Stakeholders at the panel discussion
a7053.speech: Suggested that a functioning food system is not just about producing more food, but also about making food accessible and affordable, and recommend investment in supply chains, transportation, and market infrastructure as critical to ensuring food reaches those who need it most.

a7053.speaker: Miyuki Yamashita, Head of Food Systems and Resilience at the World Food Programme
a7053.speech: “The transition from humanitarian assistance to resilience is critical. We need to focus on building food systems that support local authorities and increase coordination with diverse actors to ensure food accessibility and affordability.” ; “To achieve this, the transition must be intentional, ensuring that the most vulnerable are prioritized. Collaboration should be at the center, with active participation from all actors to foster coordination, inclusivity, and shared benefits.”

a7053.speaker: Lansana Wonneh, Programme Manager at South Sudan Women’s Social and Economic Empowerment Project (SSWSEEP), UN Women
a7053.speech: “Women play a critical role in agricultural production and social cohesion. However, they continue to face barriers such as limited access to land, finance, and decision-making spaces” ; “Addressing these inequalities requires the development of policies that support their empowerment and meaningful participation in food systems.”

a7053.speaker: Bettina Iseli, Chief Program Officer from Welthungerhilfe headquarters in Germany
a7053.speech: “We must rethink our approach. Agroecology and climate-resilient farming methods can help farmers produce more food while protecting the environment. But it will take collective action—from government, donors, and communities—to build a truly sustainable food system.”

a7053.speaker: Ania Okinczyc, Country Director of Welthungerhilfe South Sudan
a7053.speech: “Development organizations play a key role in supporting local food systems, but the real change must come from within. We need to empower farmers with the right skills, tools, and market access to make agriculture a sustainable livelihood.”

a7053.speaker: Panelists at the high-level discussion
a7053.speech: Agreed that South Sudan’s journey to food self-sufficiency requires urgent and coordinated action, and that greater security, investment in sustainable farming, and supportive policies are essential for ensuring a thriving agricultural sector.

a7251.speaker: Media Institute of Southern Africa (MISA) Malawi Chapter
a7251.speech: Reaffirmed its commitment to combating misinformation in the country through the I Verify Malawi project, an initiative which seeks to promote the dissemination of accurate information on critical issues, including the upcoming elections scheduled for September.

a7251.speaker: Steve Simba, MISA Malawi board member
a7251.speech: Speaking at a stakeholder meeting at the M'mbelwa District Council, emphasized the importance of equipping citizens with fact-checking skills, noting that these skills are essential for addressing the growing spread of fake news, which threatens informed decision-making and national unity: "The fight against misinformation is everyone's responsibility. Through this project, we aim to empower communities with the tools and knowledge they need to distinguish facts from falsehoods."

a7251.speaker: Christine Chakhumbira, Malawi Electoral Commission (MEC) officer for Mzimba South
a7251.speech: Commended the iVerify Malawi project as both timely and critical for safeguarding the integrity of information on national matters, and highlighted the importance of credible and accurate information, particularly during election periods: "This initiative comes at a crucial time when misinformation can significantly impact national interests. It is a vital step toward ensuring that citizens are well-informed and can actively participate in the democratic process."

a7348.speaker: Samuel Batcho, National Coordinator of MCA-Benin
a7348.speech: “The Millennium Challenge Corporation gives pride of place to the preservation of the environment, to health, to the safety of populations and to safeguarding the interests of the most vulnerable in all investments made under the Compact. That is why the International Finance Corporation’s performance standards on environmental and social sustainability must be applied from the design stage right through to the full implementation of the Compact.”

a7348.speaker: Samuel Batcho, National Coordinator of MCA-Benin
a7348.speech: Said the study of the population resettlement framework for the projects of Benin’s second Compact will make it possible to “collect the data, analyse it and prepare in advance any Resettlement Action Plans (RAPs) or, if needed, livelihood restoration plans and other standard chapters such as the regulatory framework, the institutional framework, the grievance redress mechanism”, and to prepare at least two sets of hypotheses (resettlement scenarios) as well as estimates of the number of people to be displaced for the Energy and Roads projects; he said the study will also make it possible to better grasp the activities planned under the next Compact and to determine the social costs to be taken into account in defining the projects of the second MCA-Benin programme.

a7348.speaker: Experts present at the workshop
a7348.speech: maintained that resettlement can be involuntary when it “refers to any resettlement where expropriation applies while the affected persons do not have the right to refuse”, or voluntary, referring in that case “to any resettlement that is not attributable to an expropriation. The operating principles of voluntary resettlement are informed consent and the option to choose.”

a7455.speaker: Jose Agnelo Sanches, economist and consultant
a7455.speech: "The joint importation by the two operators that act in the fuel sector has not structurally changed this situation, so the cost of electricity continues to be one of the highest in the world and the ship and aircraft supply sector (bunkering) is less competitive than the Canary Islands and Dakar, notwithstanding that Cabo Verde's geostrategic situation is better than that of its competitors."

a7455.speaker: Jose Agnelo Sanches, economist and consultant
a7455.speech: Has no doubt that the long-term evolution of the cost of energy is also a great threat to Cabo Verde's future competitiveness: "With the annual increase in energy demand of around 7-8%, combined with the increase in fossil fuel prices, above 10%, the cost of fuel imports has seen galloping increases, of about more than 12 times" ; stresses that if energy demand and fossil fuel prices continue at the same level this decade, import expenditure could increase around 20 times more, strongly pressuring Cabo Verde's balance of payments and the competitiveness of the national economy.

a7455.speaker: Jose Agnelo Sanches, economist and consultant
a7455.speech: "In this sense the initiatives of successive governments to work towards increasing the penetration rate of renewable energies by 50%, and studies towards an option using 100% Renewable Energy by 2050, as well as the identification of energy efficiency measures, seem very well judged."

a7455.speaker: Jose Agnelo Sanches, economist and consultant
a7455.speech: Observes that water and energy costs represent on average around 40 to 45% of production costs in Cabo Verde, with water for agriculture at around 19 to 22% and energy for catering, services and manufacturing at around 25 to 30% ; reiterates that irregularity of access, high costs and precarious availability of these two essential goods impact the whole economy, blocking production and distribution and affecting the competitiveness of products and services as well as the attractiveness of the economy as a whole.

a7455.speaker: Continuous Multi-Objective Survey (IMC-2024)
a7455.speech: 43.9% of households in Cabo Verde had access to insufficient quantities of water to satisfy their needs in 2024; the same source indicates that 52.3% of the rural population felt the need for water, a larger proportion than in urban areas.

a7455.speaker: Jose Agnelo Sanches, economist and consultant
a7455.speech: "The water problem constitutes one of Cabo Verde's greatest challenges. About 80% of the water for domestic consumption in Cabo Verde is desalinated and with a high cost of energy, with a direct implication for the water tariff, considered one of the highest in Africa."

a7455.speaker: Jose Agnelo Sanches, economist and consultant
a7455.speech: Stresses that the country has made significant progress in promoting access to drinking water, having reached the Millennium Development Goals on that matter in 2007, ahead of the 2015 target: "And we are on a good pace as regards the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals 2030, in this case SDG 6 - Clean water and sanitation... and SDG 7 - Affordable and Clean Energy" ; but says those advances mask the challenging reality of the water sector, concealing disparities between rural and urban areas: "The reality is that per capita water consumption in Cabo Verde is still below the minimums globally recommended by the WHO. It is estimated that around 30% of the country's population still does not have access to the public water supply network. On the other hand, the population that obtains supply outside the network pays a price far higher than the average price charged on the network."

a7455.speaker: Jose Agnelo Sanches, economist and consultant
a7455.speech: Admits that everything has already been identified and turned into specific programmes, such as the National Strategic Plan for Water and Sanitation (PLENAS) of 2015 and 2025, the Master Plan for the Electricity Sector, and the project "Access to Sustainable Energy for the Management of Water Resources: Energy-Water Nexus", but concludes that there remains the "enormous challenge" of timely delivery, implying an acceleration in planned investments and policy measures.

a7482.speaker: Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) (report)
a7482.speech: Has concluded that the quality, efficiency and sustainability of Botswana’s HIV response will be adversely affected by the suspension of US aid; the report anticipates poor service quality as a result of loss of trained staff and closure of drop-in centres which will ultimately place a heavy work load on government staff ; “The pause in US assistance to community programmes and drop-in centres means tens of thousands will lose access to critical services such as HIV testing, ART, PrEP and screenings for tuberculosis and sexually transmitted infections.”

a7482.speaker: UNAIDS (report)
a7482.speech: On the closure of drop-in centres, the report stated: “Most drop-in centres for key populations are closed, with only one in Gaborone partly open. This closure affects safe spaces for key populations, potentially leading to treatment default.” ; “Increased workload for government staff may hinder adequate monitoring of adherence and retention for clients on treatment. There is a risk of losing trained staff, which could lead to poorer service quality.”

a7482.speaker: UNAIDS (report)
a7482.speech: Noted that the government has set up a Joint Oversight Committee Task Team in collaboration with civil society organisations (CSOs) and other partners to monitor the impacts of the US aid suspension and to develop solutions to the problem; according to UNAIDS, the Ministry of Health is working with CSOs to ensure alternative service provision to clients whose usual drop-in centres are closed ; “Measures are being put in place to ensure that CSO-provided services that have been closed collaborate with government-funded CSOs and refer clients to government facilities.”

a7482.speaker: UNAIDS (report)
a7482.speech: “However, demand creation related to vertical transmission and pediatric HIV has been affected. UNAIDS is facilitating regular dialogues of CSOs to assess the situation and collectively decide on mitigating measures.” The report concluded that the involvement of UNAIDS and other international partners will strengthen Botswana’s HIV response in the long term.
